text: Measured: 10,000 virtual threads each sleeping 100 ms finished in 146 ms. What does that change?
choices: It makes thread pools obsolete, since unbounded thread creation is now free.
Blocking code becomes the right default again — the async machinery built to avoid blocking a scarce thread was solving a problem virtual threads mostly remove.
It means blocking calls no longer occupy a thread at all, so locks are unnecessary.
Nothing about correctness; virtual threads are also immune to race conditions.
explanation: A virtual thread costs a few hundred bytes and unmounts from its carrier when it blocks, where ten thousand platform threads would need ten thousand stacks. So the modern advice is the older advice: write blocking code, one thread per task. What it does not change is anything about shared state — they are cheaper threads, not safer ones.
